newsitem.title: USA: Dollar climbs amid signs of deep German economic slump.
newsitem.headline: Dollar climbs amid signs of deep German economic slump.

text.p: The dollar ended higher against most leading currencies Tuesday after climbing to its strongest level in 33 months against the German mark on talk that Germany's economic woes were deepening.

After trading higher throughout the session, the dollar made a late push above 1.68 marks for the first time since May 1994. A report on Market News Service Inc. cited an unidentifed source familiar with German finance officials as saying they would welcome a dollar rally to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks.

But the U.S. unit quickly surrendered those late gains as investors questioned the veracity of the report, which contradicted earlier rumours that Germany's Bundesbank had sold dollars for marks to slow the currency's ascent.

"The Market News story seemed a little far-fetched. The dollar went screaming up there (to 1.68 marks), but then turned in its tracks," said Kevin Lawrie, head of global foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.

The dollar ended higher at 1.6784 marks versus 1.6562 late Monday and at 1.4375 Swiss francs, up from 1.4257. The British pound fell to $1.6371 from $1.6428 Tuesday. The dollar rose to 123.42 Japanese yen from 122.77 and stood unchanged at Canadian $1.3552.
The mark slumped against a wide range of currencies, which helped to boost the dollar.

The German unit reached a four-year low against the British pound after a British news report projected Germany's 1997 federal budget deficit would exceed official estimates and prevent Germany from joining a proposed single European currency in 1999.
The pound also strengthened on a comment from Bank of England deputy Governor Howard Davies, who called for an increase in official British interest rates to guard against inflation.

Germany's troubled economy, struggling under its highest unemployment rate since before World War II, pales in comparison with the steadily growing U.S. economy. Investors have flocked to U.S. assets and the dollar as a result, dealers said.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reinforced that thinking with comments to the House of Representatives Ways and Means Committee. Rubin said the strong dollar had contributed to a healthy U.S. economy and kept interest rates low.

"The dollar is probably going to go higher. There is good economic fundamental support for the dollar," said Robert Nelson, managing director for foreign exchange sales at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
Yet the dollar's relatively modest rally against the yen suggested investors believe global monetary authorities will enter the market to undermine the dollar if it continues to climb, dealers said.

A series of official statements following Saturday's meeting of leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Berlin strongly hinted they would like to see the dollar stabilise near current levels.
"The market has challenged the integrity of that G7 decision and it will continue to do so until we see central bank intervention," said Nelson.
